newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia's Hun Sen seen at political crossroads.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's Hun Sen seen at political crossroads.

text.p: Cambodian strongman Hun Sen faces a difficult choice between caving in to foreign pressure or facing the possibility of plunging the country once again into isolation, analysts said on Friday.
Hun Sen realises his balancing act of courting international favour while consolidating power after his July 5 coup cannot last forever, they said.

"This is a moment of truth for him. He's got a real dilemma -- he must either appease the international community and gain legitimacy or entirely reject international pressure and face isolation," said one Cambodian political analyst.
"He wants it both ways -- control on the ground but no international interference. Yet it's hard to get support if you won't allow outside intervention."

Cambodia was isolated diplomatically from much of the world between 1975, when the Khmer Rouge instigated a Maoist experiment which left more than one million Cambodians dead, and a U.N.-brokered peace agreement in 1991.

Hun Sen was a key figure in a Vietnamese-backed government which ousted the Khmer Rouge in 1978 and ruled until U.N.-sponsored elections in 1993 led to a coalition government he shared with Prince Norodom Ranariddh.

Hun Sen, as second prime minister, overthrew First Prime Minister Ranariddh nearly two weeks ago in a bloody offensive in the capital that drew criticism from the international community and led to the postponement of Cambodia's expected entry into ASEAN later this month.

The pressure seemed to be affecting Hun Sen on Friday, the eve of a visit by three foreign ministers from the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) and the day after the United States announced it, too, was sending an envoy to Phnom Penh.
"Please do not interfere," Hun Sen said in a speech in the Cambodian countryside. "Let us solve our own problems."
Since the coup, several nations have exerted pressure on Hun Sen to put an end to the reported killing of Ranariddh loyalists and to restore the country's coalition government.
At least 40 royalist supporters have been killed in the aftermath of the prince's ouster, a U.N. official said on Friday.

Thai Foreign Minister Prachuab Chaiyasarn, Indonesia's Ali Alatas and Domingo Siazon of the Philippines were due in Phnom Penh on Saturday after meetings with King Norodom Sihanouk in Beijing and Ranariddh in Bangkok.
The United States said on Thursday it would send former U.S. congressman Stephen Solarz to Asia to pursue a coordinated resolution of the Cambodian crisis.
Solarz will leave on Friday or Saturday for a trip to Beijing, Tokyo, Bangkok, Jakarta, Kuala Lumpur and Phnom Penh, where he will meet Hun Sen, the U.S. State Department said.

But Asian diplomats and political analysts expressed doubt that Solarz's trip would do much to change Hun Sen's position. He has repeatedly said it is up to Cambodians, not foreigners, to solve their own problems.
"I don't think it will do much," said one foreign analyst of the U.S. envoy's visit.
An Asian diplomat said Solarz's visit may complicate ASEAN's efforts to negotiate a solution to Cambodia's political crisis.
"I don't think this is a good idea. The government is moving toward normalcy and this will just confuse the effort," the diplomat said, suggesting Hun Sen could take only so much advice.
What will prove more effective, analysts said, was the leverage ASEAN's three envoys will gain from Hun Sen's desire to win acceptance into the regional club as soon as possible.
But ASEAN's patience is running out as well, the diplomat said.

"The government didn't follow through on its promises (to maintain stability). This has been a slap to ASEAN, and some members aren't in a hurry to have them join so quickly," said the diplomat. "ASEAN needs to see Hun Sen meet them halfway."
